Protocol Security

Lightning Network Under Pressure as Node Exploits and Infrastructure Breaches Strike in Tandem

Core Lightning operators scramble to patch dual-funding and splice flaws while custodial systems trace funds to a single persistent adversary.

By Fanis and our Infrastructure Desk · [s520]

The past several weeks have tested node runners and custodial rails across the Lightning ecosystem with uncommon severity. According to Fanis in the newly resumed Latest Strikes newsletter, node operators face an intense race between the good and the bad guys that has already led to confirmed fund theft across active routing channels [s520].

Two distinct defects in Core Lightning have been actively exploited in the wild. The first involves dual-funded channel construction, where an attacker executes a replacement-by-fee (RBF) maneuver on a funding transaction after the initial transaction confirmed but before channel acknowledgement. When the peer signals readiness, the victim node recalculates capacity from the phantom transaction and attributes fake liquidity to the counterparty, allowing genuine funds to be drained from other channels. While patched in commit 5a77a0e, existing affected channels must be suspended with close <id> 0 to halt further theft [s520].

The second vulnerability strikes splicing logic, where a forced close executed after a splice locks but before memory references clear mistakenly relies on obsolete commitments, permitting an adversary to claim the entire balance with a penalty transaction. Beyond node software, the ecosystem faces coordinated operational attacks: on September 19, an adversary accessed an administrative interface at Blink to alter credentials on 35 accounts, followed on October 5 by an exploit against Second's Ark boarding flow. Forensics published by Blink confirmed that both intrusions originated from the exact same Lightning node [s520].

Grassroots Operations

Freeing Meetups from Big Tech Dues

Why paying monthly platform fees contradicts sovereign principles when an open Nostr stack costs five dollars.

By BITKARROT · [s540]

According to BITKARROT in an urgent operational appeal, Your Bitcoin meetup is paying Meetup.com $30 a month to exist. Meanwhile, you believe in decentralized money, censorship-resistant protocols, and self-sovereignty. One of these things is not like the others. [s540]

The solution requires neither proprietary services nor rare developer talent. Any local gathering can deploy a dedicated community relay on a five-dollar virtual server, publish event calendars as discoverable Nostr notes, issue member identities over NIP-05, and circulate satoshis directly within local commerce circles. As BITKARROT observes, decentralization that exists only on paper is a slogan—and communities that rely on centralized directories invite eventual eviction [s540].

Interface Architecture

A Text Standard for Designers and Agents

By Vladimir Krstić · [s5], [s12]

The friction between graphical canvas tools and production software remains one of modern computing's most stubborn divides. Today's design software typically offers static exports that misunderstand target architecture and sever synchronization the moment source files diverge.

Vladimir Krstić outlines an alternative standard built on plain text: The idea is to have a design file that both humans and agents can read and edit [s5]. By storing layouts, components, and design tokens in human-readable .elyx files, interface specifications can sit inside version control repositories alongside application logic. Designers edit visually, while developers and agents can read and edit the same files directly [s12].

Dispatches, Software & The Wire

Client Engineering

Unlocking the Hidden Capabilities of Amethyst

By ‌Đee Kay · [s518], [s519]

Most mobile users treat their Nostr clients as simple microblogging portals, yet contemporary clients conceal full transactional operating systems beneath their default toggles. In an exhaustive technical reference manual, Đee Kay examines Amethyst v1.17.0, showing that the Android client's payment engine extends well beyond standard lightning bolts.

There is an entire payment feature in #amethyst waiting behind a single switch, because it ships turned off [s518]. Enabling payment targets permits profiles to present chips for Cash App, Nano, Revolut, BIP-352 silent payments, and BIP-353 human-readable identifiers. Furthermore, the client manages four parallel wallet tiers—NWC, CLINK debits, Cashu ecash, and native on-chain Taproot wallets—enabling multi-rail liquidity settlement directly inside discussion threads [s518].

Encrypted Messaging

Private Chat Upgrades on iOS and Android

By White Noise · [s533]

Private messaging network White Noise delivered major dual-platform updates today. The iOS release introduces opt-in link previews (kept disabled by default to prevent IP exposure to external hosts) and animated GIF rendering. The Android build increases supported transfer sizes for documents and videos up to 512 MB, with local on-device translation managed through an offline translation tool [s533].
